item.title: New Research Says the AI Gender Gap Has Closed. Has It?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

New Research Says the AI Gender Gap Has Closed. Has It?

The real gender gap in AI tells an important story about access and visibility.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • New research finds women and men report similar rates of ever using AI, although men use it more regularly.
  • Women receive less AI training, mentorship, and encouragement at work than men.
  • Women are far less visible than men in news coverage on AI experts.
  • Almost 50% of survey respondents claimed they recognized two ficticious names who were purportedly AI experts.

Have you heard of these individuals: Craig Dalton, Fei-Fei Li, Mira Murati, and Susan Millner? From the title of this piece, you might infer that they have something to do with the gender gap in AI—and you’d be, well, partially right.

For the past few years, the media has highlighted that fewer women than men use AI tools. But does the gender gap in AI still exist? Two new reports, released just two days apart last week, came to seemingly contradictory conclusions. Both drew on surveys of more than 5,000 U.S. adults conducted in 2026.

A Pew Research Center report noted that the gender gap in the use of AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT, has closed and that women’s use of AI has increased steeply over the past two years. According to the report, similar shares of women (47%) and men (50%) now use AI chatbots.

Another report, released two days earlier by the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School, concluded that women (29%) were more likely than men (22%) to report that they had never used an AI tool.

How can we make sense of the discrepancy between these reports? The wording of the surveys—“AI chatbots” versus “AI tools”—may have made a difference. The surveys also used different sampling methodologies. The Pew Research Center, for example, used a nationally representative panel of U.S. adults.

But when I dug deeper into the reports, I found that their conclusions were more similar than different. The Shorenstein report identified no statistically significant gender difference in whether people had ever used AI when the researchers examined desktop browsing data, which measured people’s actual behavior.

The Real Gender Gap

But has the gender gap in AI really closed? Asking whether someone has ever used an AI tool may not be particularly meaningful. After all, a person could try an AI tool, decide they don’t trust or like it, and never use it again. A more useful metric may be whether women and men use AI regularly.

On this point, the reports agree. The Pew report found that men use AI chatbots daily more often than women do (27% versus 20%). Likewise, the Shorenstein report found that 25% of men used AI regularly, compared with only 16% of women. So, when it comes to regular or daily use, a gender gap persists. But why?

Here again, both reports provide useful insights. According to the Pew report, women are more likely than men to believe that AI will negatively affect them personally and society more broadly. Likewise, the Shorenstein report found that women trusted AI less than men did and were more likely to associate it with anxiety and worry. Overall, women expressed more negative attitudes toward AI than men did.

Gender Inequities Persist

The Shorenstein report provides additional evidence that helps explain the gender gap in AI use. Among employed respondents, women were more likely than men to report receiving no AI training at work (64% versus 49%). Women also reported receiving less mentoring and encouragement related to AI use.

Both women and men in the Shorenstein survey perceived men as better represented than women in AI news, development, and content. Men also dominated news coverage and public discussions about AI. Across 78,542 U.S. news articles, men appeared in headlines 14.6 times as often as women. Among experts cited in those articles, men were cited 4.3 times as often as women.

This brings us to the most stunning findings in the Shorenstein report. Participants were asked whether they recognized the names of several influential figures in AI development. The list included both women and men. For every name on the list, men were more likely than women to report recognizing the person.

Technology leaders Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg were recognized by more than 90% of respondents. By contrast, Daniela Amodei—the most widely recognized woman on the list—was recognized by only 49%, slightly less than Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei, the least widely recognized men, at 50% each.

Unbeknownst to the respondents, however, the researchers had slipped two fictitious names into the list of AI experts: Craig Dalton and Susan Millner. And here’s the kicker: Fei-Fei Li and Mira Murati, two influential women in AI development, were each recognized by only 46% of respondents—the same percentage who reported recognizing the two fabricated names. This finding underscores how invisible even some of the most influential women in AI remain to the public.

The Takeaway

The take-home message from these reports is not that women should be encouraged to use AI more often. There are likely good reasons to be cautious about using AI and its potential negative effects. The greater concern is the broader systemic gender inequity. We need to ask hard questions about whether women have equal opportunities to understand AI, shape its development, and influence the public conversation surrounding it.

The Shorenstein report explicitly recommends that organizations and employers do more to provide women with the support and information they need to decide how and when to use AI in the workplace. Journalists and news organizations can also widen the pool of experts they consult. If women do not see themselves represented in news about AI, is it any surprise that they use AI less regularly and remain more skeptical about its benefits?

Reflections on Fabricated Names

I’ll conclude with a broader point that extends beyond the gender gap in AI. Almost half of the Shorenstein survey respondents reported recognizing the fabricated names Craig Dalton and Susan Millner as AI experts. And men (53%) were more likely than women (40%) to make this claim, even though the two names are wholly fictitious.

Wow. How do we even make sense of that?

I suspect that in a culture that prizes certainty and confidence, admitting that one does not recognize an influential AI figure can feel like a weakness. And perhaps men struggle with this problem more than women do.

But acknowledging uncertainty and recognizing the limitations of one’s knowledge should be viewed as strengths. These are markers of intellectual humility—an attribute that research has shown helps people make sound decisions, resist misinformation, and relate better to others.

I don’t know. I could be wrong. I need more time to figure this out. These words may not project confidence. But they embody the qualities we need in a rapidly changing, AI-shaped world in which bold assertions often outpace genuine understanding.

item.title: New Study Explores How Antizionism Coincides With Antisemitism
item.description:
Bias

New Study Explores How Antizionism Coincides With Antisemitism

Does antizionism produce the patterns of prejudice that psychology can measure?

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • In a new study, antizionism coincided with recognizable markers of anti-Jewish prejudice.
  • Antizionist sentiment correlated with hostility toward average Israelis
  • Antizionist sentiment predicted anti-Jewish double standards in policy scenarios
Source: rhk.photo via Pexels

The discourse over whether antizionism is antisemitic has reached an impasse.

One side argues that these are two sides of the same coin. Denying Israel’s legitimacy, demonizing its supporters, or applying standards to it that are not applied to any other country constitutes a modern form of antisemitism. Critics of that position respond that antizionism is a political viewpoint, and labeling it as antisemitic is to effectively silence legitimate criticism of Israel’s government or military actions. The argument then circles back to competing definitions, with neither side convincing the other.

I set out to examine this topic empirically, hypothesizing that antizionist attitudes might coincide with familiar markers of prejudice, including overlap with traditional Judeophobic antisemitism, hostility toward civilians, racialized moral judgments, and double standards. We now have evidence published in the journal Current Psychology which is consistent with all of those patterns, drawing on survey data from 3 volunteer samples totaling 2,256 (mostly college-educated and somewhat left-leaning) adult participants.

Building off previous work, my student and I measured two related but also distinct constructs, traditional Judeophobic antisemitism (including stereotypes about Jewish greed or conspiratorial power) and Antizionist antisemitism, which taps into delegitimization or demonization of Israel and its supporters, and the application of differential standards relative to other nations. This goes well beyond mere criticism of an Israeli government or policy. In all 3 samples we collected, a positive correlation emerged between these variables. This means that these two types of anti-Jewish attitudes overlapped considerably, although they were not completely interchangeable.

We also observed that antizionist sentiment was strongly associated with perceiving average Israelis (i.e., not IDF soldiers or politicians) as immoral (e.g., disgusting, untrustworthy, malevolent) and as oppressors. Left-wing political attitudes were also correlated with hostile attitudes toward average Israelis.

Interestingly, participants tended to view Israelis as whiter than Palestinians, regardless of how much they espoused antizionist viewpoints. And the more strongly participants perceived Israelis as white, the more they also viewed them as privileged and oppressive. But antizionist attitudes also played a role alongside ethnicity. Among those participants who scored high on antizionist sentiment, perceiving Israelis as white was associated with thinking of them as more immoral. Furthermore, among those participants with left-wing political attitudes, perceiving Israelis as whiter than Palestinians also correlated with greater support for Palestine over Israel and stronger antizionist sentiment.

These results suggest that viewing Middle Eastern peoples through a zero-sum, oppressor-versus-oppressed framework goes hand in hand with casting Israeli civilians in the role of “white oppressor” villains, and judging them in more dehumanizing terms.

The final part of our research examined double-standards. We were inspired by similar experimental studies by other researchers attempting to understand these dynamics. We randomly assigned participants to evaluate otherwise identical policy scenarios involving different target groups. One scenario asked whether Americans’ emotional ties to another country created a conflict of interest. Some participants read about Jewish Americans and Israel, while others read about Hispanic Americans and Mexico. Additional policy scenarios involved military service in foreign countries (Israel or Ukraine), academic boycotts (Israel or Russia), and national-identity laws (Israel, Jordan, or Denmark).

When these policy questions were framed as involving Jews and/or Israel, participants expressed harsher judgment if they also held antizionist attitudes. Importantly, our results revealed a pattern of double standards across many, but not all of the policy scenarios we used; some of them produced null effects. But when correlations did emerge between antizionist viewpoints and double standards, they always went in the same direction, which was consistently against the Jewish people.

Taken together, our data consistently show that the antizionist construct we measured repeatedly exhibited markers associated with other forms of group prejudice. This includes (1) a positive correlation with Judeophobic attitudes, (2) animosity toward Israeli civilians, (3) viewing Israelis more negatively as a function of their perceived ethnicity, and (4) anti-Jewish double-standards in policy scenarios.

This does not mean that antizionism and antisemitism are the exact same thing. Our findings are compatible with Adam Louis-Klein’s formulation of antizionism as a form of anti-Jewish bigotry that is psychologically distinct from traditional Judeophobic antisemitism. The discourse around how and whether antizionism “crosses the line into antisemitism” misses the point. Our research cannot deduce whether every antizionist belief is antisemitic. But it does show that the form of antizionist sentiment we measured consistently coincided with recognizable markers of anti-Jewish bias.

There is a practical lesson here as well, for all readers, regardless of their feelings toward Jews or Israel. When evaluating whether a political argument has become infused with prejudice, try imagining how you would react if the target was any other group of people, especially another minority group. Would a strong emotional attachment to another ancestral homeland also constitute disloyalty to one’s home country? Would it be morally correct to support an academic boycott of scholars in another country whose government takes actions you find reprehensible? If the answer to those questions changes when the target group changes, then the attitude is not clearly resting on a consistent principle or policy, and may instead rest on prejudice. This should prompt some serious reflection.

Instead of continuing an irreconcilable deliberation over whether antizionism is antisemitic, we could pivot to ask a more concrete and straightforward question: Does antizionism coincide with animosity toward average Israelis, ethnic-based prejudice, or unequal ethical standards? Whatever label one ultimately prefers for such a belief system, those patterns deserve to be confronted as a form of prejudice.

item.title: How to Choose a Faithful Partner
item.description:
Infidelity

How to Choose a Faithful Partner

Personality types prompt perception of unfaithful behavior.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Partners have different ideas of what unfaithful behavior looks like.
  • Dark personalities view infidelity differently than other people.
  • Some people judge their own behavior more permissively than a partner's behavior.
Source: Image by Mohamed Chermiti from Pixabay

“It was just coffee,” a partner might proclaim, when their significant other views an extramarital meetup as more about the company than the caffeine. The same type of conversation might follow emotionally intimate text messages or emails, with the sender explaining, “We were just talking.” So where is the line? As these examples illustrate, one of the most significant issues faced by romantic partners is agreeing on what type of behavior constitutes infidelity. The answer may depend on everything from personal commitment to personality. Research explains.

Infidelity, Personality, and Personal Perception

Gayle Brewer et al. (2023) examined the issue of perceptions of infidelity in a piece aptly entitled “But It Wasn’t Really Cheating.”[i] They acknowledge that some acts are easier to identify than others, noting that sexual intercourse is generally thought to constitute infidelity while opinions about sending affectionate texts or emails are more diverse. They also note, however, that the extent to which specific acts are viewed as infidelity may impact both responses to the behavior of a partner and willingness to engage in these behaviors personally. Accordingly, they examined the proclivities and perceptions of romantic infidelity among individuals with different types of personalities.

Brewer et al. recognized five categories of infidelity: 1) online, 2) fantasized, 3) emotional, 4) sexual, and 5) hidden attachment. In their research, they found the Dark Triad traits of Machiavellianism and primary psychopathy predicted how distinct acts were perceived as infidelity, controlling for personal experience and demographic factors. Specifically, they found that people high on Machiavellianism, a personality type characterized by manipulation and a willingness to exploit other people, were less likely to perceive expressing emotion or fantasizing as infidelity. They found that people scoring high on primary psychopathy, involving emotional jealousy, among other things, were more likely to perceive emotional expression and fantasizing as infidelity yet less likely to view sexual behavior or hidden attachment as demonstrations of unfaithfulness.

Previous research has revealed similar results regarding the link between personality and perception of infidelity.

Infidelity and Hypocrisy

Ashley E. Thompson and Lucia F. O’Sullivan examined inconsistent explanations of infidelity in a piece aptly entitled “I Can But You Can’t.”[ii] Using online surveys with 810 adults, they examined the differences between the way people defined infidelity, comparing their opinions about their own behavior to the behavior of their partners. They found that participants judged their own behavior more permissively than the behavior of their partners, yet only in the area of emotional/affectionate and technology/online behaviors, not behavior categorized as sexual/explicit or solitary.

Many study participants reported having themselves been unfaithful, indulging in behavior they judged as infidelity, particularly in the categories of emotional/affectionate and technology/online. Thompson and O’Sullivan noted that inconsistent judgments of infidelity and self-reported behavior (hypocrisy) depended on factors including age, religion, and sexual attitudes.

Personality Predicts Relational Permanence

Thompson and O’Sullivan found that gender did not predict consistency in comparing judgments and behavior, but dark personality traits did. They observed that hypocrisy has been associated with personality traits such as Machiavellianism, which they define as manipulative behavior, focusing on self-interest over the interests of others. They emphasize that variables which capture personality traits may be a better judge of consistency between judgments and behavior than demographic variables such as gender, which is valuable advice for people seeking a faithful partner.

Accordingly, before rushing into a relationship, instead of falling for gender-based stereotypes, take the time to explore the personality behind the persona. Early daters are on their best behavior, but people cannot hide personality traits such as manipulative tendencies or callousness for very long. Thoughtful relationship choices produce quality pairings that endure and flourish over time.

item.title: Feeling Vulnerable vs. Being Vulnerable
item.description:
Emotions

Feeling Vulnerable vs. Being Vulnerable

The hidden powers of feeling vulnerable.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling vulnerable is an internal state, but doesn't imply that you're actually unsafe or threatened.
  • Being vulnerable means you both feel exposed and believe you're at actual risk of harm.
  • Confusing vulnerability with danger limits growth, creativity, and emotional intimacy.
Source: Oleksil Bocharov/Unsplash

We’re often not clear about our relationship with vulnerability. Thanks to Brené Brown's work, vulnerability holds a more honored place in the human experience. She calls vulnerability “the birthplace of love, belonging, joy, courage, empathy, and creativity.” However, when people confuse feeling vulnerable with being vulnerable, vulnerability loses some of its appeal. Let’s look more closely at these two different experiences of vulnerability.

Feeling Vulnerable

Feeling vulnerable is an internal experience that may include tenderness, sweetness, fear, openheartedness, weakness, fragility, feeling lost or inadequate, feeling loving or kindhearted, and being touched and moved. The belief that accompanies feeling vulnerable is “I’m safe” or “There’s no reason to believe that I will be emotionally or physically harmed.” However, that doesn’t suggest we will feel secure and comfortable as we move from our many ideas into our hearts.

It’s quite a journey, this trip from head to heart. Our minds are a place of sanctuary. We create stories about allegedly being peaceful, safe, and rewarded. There are stories about how your partner and your friends will treat you, what will happen tomorrow, and who will get the promotion at work. When we open our hearts, we temporarily separate from that mental reassurance, feeling less at ease and more concerned.

If I am about to speak to someone with an open heart, I must trust that the listener will respond kindly. Let’s say that I have good reason to believe that the listener will respond with empathy. However, the listener reacts defensively and makes aggressive accusations. The situation has just shifted from my feeling vulnerable to being vulnerable or subjected to emotional hurt. I hope I can muster enough resilience to set boundaries protecting me from the attack. A situation can move from feeling vulnerable to being vulnerable. I don’t want to avoid feeling vulnerable because of the change that can happen. The more I trust that I will take care of myself if a shift happens, the more I give myself permission to feel vulnerable.

Being Vulnerable

Being vulnerable includes feeling vulnerable accompanied by the belief that I am not safe or I’m being subjected to either an emotional or physical threat. As mentioned above, a situation can move from feeling vulnerable to being vulnerable as the listener begins making disparaging remarks about my character.

Several events can leave us vulnerable: A truck bearing down on you as you’re crossing a street, living in the path of a tornado, experiencing a home invasion, being in an unexpected storm at sea, brakes becoming inoperable while driving, being in a house that catches fire, or being diagnosed with a catastrophic illness.

Feeling vulnerable can be difficult to distinguish from being vulnerable. As children, when we feel fear, we almost automatically decide we’re not safe. It’s only too easy to recreate “if I’m scared, then I’m not safe” in adulthood. As a result, whenever we feel vulnerable and scared, we believe we’re unsafe. It takes practice to interrupt this coupling between feeling vulnerable and believing we’re unsafe. It’s appropriate to believe we’re not safe when we’re being vulnerable, so we can take action to protect ourselves.

Some Advantages

There are several significant advantages to feeling vulnerable and safe.

  • Creativity. We can access new vision as we step away from the status quo or conventional prescriptions. Creativity isn't an option when we’re being vulnerable, since that suggests we’re in survival mode, limiting our choices to fight, flee, or freeze.
  • Unity consciousness. Our different ideologies and political positions tend to separate us, while kindheartednes and other vulnerable feelings are common to all of us.
  • Empathy. The more permission we give ourselves to feel vulnerable, the more we can identify with others' feelings.
  • Authenticity. When we feel vulnerable, we move away from pretense and strategic posturing. We are more likely to be ourselves, represented by uncensored feelings.
  • Presence. Feeling vulnerable deepens our capacity to be present, beyond what feels appropriate.
  • A rapport builder. When we feel vulnerable with others, we reveal ourselves without filters, which encourages trust. Feeling vulnerable can easily be a building block for emotional intimacy.

To have more experiences of feeling vulnerable and benefit from the consequences means interrupting the link between feeling vulnerable and feeling unsafe. This link is natural in childhood because children are aware of how powerless they are. It also helps to notice that the discomfort that accompanies feeling vulnerable simply comes from moving away from the head toward the heart.
